ceb.title: Sola Scriptura Refutes Itself
ceb.question: Where does the Bible teach that Scripture alone is the sole authority for Christians?
ceb.answer: Nowhere does the Bible teach 'Scripture alone,' which makes the doctrine self-refuting: a rule of faith that demands biblical proof cannot itself be proven from the Bible. The verse most often cited, 2 Tim 3:16-17, says Scripture is inspired and profitable for teaching and makes the believer complete, but 'profitable' and 'useful' are not the same as 'sufficient by itself'; prayer and good works are also called profitable without excluding everything else. Paul commands the Thessalonians to hold fast to traditions delivered both orally and in writing (2 Thes 2:15), placing oral Tradition on par with written word. He calls the Church, not the Bible, the pillar and foundation of truth (1 Tim 3:15). The Bible presupposes a teaching Church that determined its own canon, so Scripture and Tradition together, under the Magisterium, form the rule of faith.

en.answer_full:
> "The holy scriptures cannot teach us without a teacher."
> — St. Jerome, *Commentary on Galatians*, Prologue (c. AD 387)

The claim that the Bible alone, interpreted without recourse to Church authority or tradition, is the sole rule of Christian faith is the cornerstone of Protestant theology — and yet, paradoxically, it is a claim nowhere found in the Bible itself. *Sola scriptura* is a tradition that contradicts itself: it makes a doctrinal claim that Scripture does not support, about a method of interpretation that Scripture itself does not prescribe.

---

## The Main Proof Text: 2 Timothy 3:16–17

*"All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that one who belongs to God may be competent, equipped for every good work."* (2 Timothy 3:16–17, NABRE)

This text says Scripture is *theopneustos* (God-breathed) and *ōphelimos* (useful). What it does not say: that Scripture is the *only* rule of faith, that tradition is invalid, or that Church authority is unnecessary. *Useful* is not *exclusively sufficient*. Medicine is useful for health; that does not mean it alone is sufficient for every health need. When Paul writes "scripture" here he means primarily the Old Testament — the New Testament canon had not yet been established. The epistemological claim of *sola scriptura* cannot be derived from this verse without importing assumptions the text does not contain.

---

## What Scripture Teaches About Authority

### 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — Oral Tradition as Binding

*"Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught, either by an oral statement or by a letter of ours."* (2 Thessalonians 2:15, NABRE)

Paul places oral apostolic tradition on the same level as his written letters — both are binding. This passage directly refutes *sola scriptura*. The Greek *paradosis* (traditions) is the authoritative handing-on of teaching, not human customs.

### 1 Timothy 3:15 — The Church as Pillar of Truth

*"But if I should be delayed, you should know how to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth."* (1 Timothy 3:15, NABRE)

Paul identifies the *Church* — not the Bible — as the *"pillar and foundation of truth."* If *sola scriptura* were true, Scripture would need to name itself as the pillar of truth. It does not — it names the Church.

### Luke 10:16 — The Church as Christ's Voice

*"Whoever listens to you listens to me. Whoever rejects you rejects me."* (Luke 10:16, NABRE)

Jesus binds his own authority to those he sends. Rejecting the apostolic teaching office is rejecting Christ himself.

### Matthew 18:17 — The Church as Final Arbiter

*"If he refuses to listen to them, tell the church. If he refuses to listen even to the church, then treat him as you would a Gentile or a tax collector."* (Matthew 18:17, NABRE)

The final authority in doctrinal disputes is the Church — not an individual's scriptural interpretation.

---

## The Self-Defeating Problem: Who Defined the Canon?

The New Testament canon was determined by Church councils:

| Council | Date | Action |
|---------|------|--------|
| Council of Rome | AD 382 | 27-book NT canon under Pope Damasus I |
| Council of Hippo | AD 393 | Affirmed the canon |
| Council of Carthage | AD 397 | Reaffirmed |
| Council of Trent | AD 1546 | Defined against Protestant deletion of the deuterocanonicals |

Every Protestant who accepts a 27-book New Testament is accepting the authority of these Catholic councils. *Sola scriptura* is logically dependent on Church authority — the very authority it claims to replace.

---

## Church Fathers

> "I would not believe the Gospel except as moved by the authority of the Catholic Church."
> — St. Augustine of Hippo, *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus Called Fundamental*, Chapter 5 (c. AD 397)

Augustine's point is epistemological: Church authority is logically prior to scriptural authority in the order of knowing. Before you can trust what the Gospel says, you must trust the community that identified the Gospel.

> "Where will you find in the Scriptures the word Trinity? If you object, Scripture does not say to baptize in the name of Father and Son and Holy Ghost, but only in the name of Jesus — these things are derived from the unwritten tradition."
> — St. Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, 27.66 (c. AD 375)

Basil identifies key Christian doctrines — including the Trinitarian baptismal formula — as derived from unwritten apostolic tradition, not Scripture alone.

> "The holy scriptures cannot teach us without a teacher."
> — St. Jerome, *Commentary on Galatians*, Prologue (c. AD 387)

Jerome, the great scripture scholar who produced the Vulgate, recognized that the text is not self-interpreting. The teacher — the Church — is required.

---

## Ecumenical Council: Council of Trent (1546)

> *"This truth and rule are contained in the written books and in the unwritten traditions which, received by the Apostles from the mouth of Christ himself, or from the Apostles themselves, the Holy Ghost dictating, have come down even unto us."*
> — Council of Trent, Session IV (1546)

Trent affirms that divine revelation comes through *both* Scripture and apostolic Tradition — not Scripture alone.

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 80 | Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture make up a single sacred deposit of the Word of God |
| CCC 85 | The task of authentically interpreting the Word of God has been entrusted solely to the Magisterium |
| CCC 95 | Tradition, Scripture, and the Magisterium are so linked that one cannot stand without the others |
| CCC 113 | Scripture is to be read in the Spirit in which it was written — in the living Tradition of the Church |

---

## Common Objections

**"The Bereans searched the Scriptures — Paul commends this as the model." (Acts 17:11)**

The Bereans examined the Old Testament to verify Paul's oral preaching. This is scripture study alongside apostolic teaching — the Catholic model. It is not scripture as the *sole* authority replacing apostolic teaching; the Bereans were checking Paul's proclamation, not substituting their private reading for it.

**"Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for their traditions — tradition is unreliable."**

Jesus rebuked *human traditions that contradicted God's command* (Mark 7:8–9) — not apostolic traditions that *carry* God's command. Paul uses the same word *paradosis* to commend the traditions he transmitted (2 Thessalonians 2:15, 1 Corinthians 11:2). The question is not whether it is tradition but whether it is apostolic.

**"Every doctrine should be tested against Scripture."**

Catholics fully agree. Every doctrine must be *consistent* with Scripture. The Catholic position is not that the Magisterium overrides Scripture — it is that the Magisterium authentically interprets Scripture within the tradition in which Scripture was produced. The Church is not above the Word of God; she is its servant and interpreter.

---

*Sola scriptura* is a doctrine that Scripture does not teach, history does not support, and five centuries of Protestant fragmentation have not validated. The Bible is the uniquely inspired Word of God — but it is the Church's book, produced within the apostolic community, defined by Church councils, and faithfully interpreted by the living Magisterium. Scripture and Tradition together, under the Magisterium, constitute the single deposit of the Christian faith.
